summary: Introduces LEANN, a low-storage vector index for embedding-based search on personal devices. Highlights storage challenges where indexes can exceed raw data size. Proposes recomputation and graph pruning to achieve less than 5% storage overhead while maintaining accuracy.

Background on approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search and graph-based methods like HNSW. Describes storage and computational challenges when deploying on consumer devices, motivating LEANN’s approach.

Outlines LEANN’s design: recompute embeddings at query time instead of storing them, and prune graph metadata by preserving high-degree nodes. Introduces two-level search and dynamic batching to reduce latency.
Details two-level search algorithm: uses approximate distances for broad exploration and exact distances for promising candidates, reducing recomputation cost. Employs PQ compression for efficiency.
Explains dynamic batching: groups nodes until GPU-efficient batch size is reached, improving utilization. Draws parallels to beam search in DiskANN but optimized for GPU recomputation.
Introduces high-degree preserving graph pruning algorithm. Retains hub nodes while reducing overall edges, significantly cutting metadata size without hurting search quality.
Evaluation setup: describes dataset (RPJ-Wiki, 76GB), embeddings, hardware (NVIDIA A10, Apple M1), and benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, GPQA, HotpotQA). Defines metrics: storage, latency, and accuracy.

Presents main evaluation results. LEANN reduces storage to <5% of raw data while keeping latency under 2s at 90% recall. Outperforms baselines like DiskANN, HNSW, IVF, and BM25 in storage–latency trade-offs.
Shows downstream RAG accuracy results. LEANN achieves higher accuracy than BM25 and PQ-compression. On datasets like NQ and TriviaQA, it delivers strong exact match and F1 improvements.
Ablation study: two-level search speeds up retrieval by ~1.4×; adding batching further improves performance up to 2×. Pruning preserves accuracy better than random pruning or naïve degree reduction.
Analyzes degree distribution in pruned graphs. LEANN’s pruning retains hub nodes, preserving connectivity and efficiency, unlike heuristic pruning methods that degrade recall.
Evaluates impact of embedding model size. Smaller models reduce latency with minor accuracy loss. Tests caching strategy: storing embeddings for hub nodes speeds up queries further.
Breaks down recomputation costs: GPU embedding generation dominates latency (~76%). Suggests overlapping I/O, CPU, and GPU to optimize further. Compares cache hit rates under different disk budgets.

Related work: reviews IVF, HNSW, DiskANN, and other ANN search methods. Summarizes compression and disk-based strategies, noting their limitations in balancing storage and accuracy on constrained devices.

Discusses broader applicability of LEANN’s recomputation and pruning techniques. Notes limitation: embeddings must still be computed once for index construction. Suggests storage-efficient build strategies.
Outlines future directions: faster GPUs and smaller embedding models will reduce latency further. Envisions extending LEANN to datacenter-scale systems to tackle embedding storage burdens.

Conclusion: LEANN achieves 50× storage reduction while maintaining accuracy and latency for ANN search on edge devices. Combines recomputation, two-level search, batching, and pruning into a practical system.
